newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-DARK CLOUDS GATHERING DOWN BY THE RIVERSIDE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DARK CLOUDS GATHERING DOWN BY THE RIVERSIDE.

text.p: Middlesbrough, the only team in the premier league who have never won a major honour, are on the verge of finally getting their name into the record books -- as the most expensive flops in English soccer history.

Fifteen months and 30 million pounds ($50.2 million) after a 30-piece Samba band greeted the arrival of the Brazilian Juninho -- followed by compatriots Emerson and Branco and the Italian Fabrizio Ravanelli -- Middlesbrough have plummeted to the bottom of the table. Even Ravanelli is tipping them for the drop with almost half the season still to play.

While Ravanelli's remarks did nothing to help team spirit on Tuesday, another development was potentially far more damaging. Middlesbrough had three points taken off their already meagre total of 18 to leave them on 15 -- four less than second-from-bottom Southampton.

That punishment, and a 50,000 pound ($83,300) fine from the league's disciplinary committee, was imposed because they failed to fulfil a fixture with Blackburn on December 21. Instead of asking for the match to be postponed because they had 23 players either ill or injured, Middlesbrough unilaterally pulled out of the game.

That incident, the fine, the points penalty, Ravanelli's remarks about relegation -- "the situation here is truly tragic" -- all point to one thing. That the dream of turning Middlesbrough into a soccer power is rapidly turning into a nightmare. The club have a superb new 30,000 capacity all-seater stadium, an ambitious millionaire chairman who is still in his 30s, and in manager Bryan Robson, one of the outstanding players of his generation.

Indeed, Robson even pulled on his boots for probably the last time in a career that has spanned over 20 years when he played against Arsenal 10 days short of his 40th birthday, on New Years Day. How Middlesbrough could do with the Robson of his great "Captain Marvel" days now.
For Robson had true grit, passion and bravery as a player, qualities they now need to show in abundance to survive.
When he left Manchester United in 1994, his first objective as manager was to steer Middlesbrough into the premier league, a feat he achieved in his first season.
Back among the elite, Middlesbrough stunned everyone in October 1995 when they signed Brazil's outstanding young player, the 22-year-old Juninho, from Sao Paulo for 4.5 million pounds ($7.5 million).

The move was greeted with barely concealed astonishment. Middlesbrough might have had a new stadium and a famous new manager, but had never been remotely fashionable -- not even in the north-east of England where they have always been the third club behind Newcastle and Sunderland.
That signing sparked scenes never before seen on Teesside.

No-one could find Brazilian hats so fans adopted Mexican sombreros instead. Fast-food stalls outside the Riverside Stadium started selling "Juninho Burgers" with "hot samba sauce". Brazilian flags were displayed in shop windows. A Samba band greeted Juninho on his debut against Leeds. Helicopters flew over the stadium trailing greetings messages.

After a century of staggering under-achievement and just nine years after officially, but temporarily, being closed down because of insolvency, Middlesbrough seemed on the verge of a bright new future.

It did not end with the signing of Juninho. Compatriots Branco and Emerson followed soon after, but the most staggering transfer of all was the arrival of Ravanelli from European champions Juventus for 7.5 million pounds ($12.5 million) in the close season. While fantasy and reality sometimes get blurred in soccer, this move was one that seemed almost surreal.
Of course, his reported salary of 20,000 pounds ($35,000) a week, played no little part, but even so, the sight of Ravanelli playing for Middlesbrough takes some getting used to.

At the start of the season all seemed to be working well. Ravanelli earned an instant place in the hearts of his new fans with a hat-trick on the opening day in a 3-3 draw against Liverpool. Although Boro failed to win their next two matches, they won the next three in a row and by mid-September were sixth.

Ravanelli could not stop scoring, but then suddenly, after hitting four in a 7-0 drubbing of lowly Hereford in the league cup, it all started going badly wrong. Branco, signed very much as Juninho's "minder", left after only 10 appearances. Emerson and his wife were finding it hard to settle in the north-east and he went back to Brazil without permission and earned himself a hefty fine on his return.

Middlesbrough started losing and by the middle of October Robson admitted that his plan of playing Juninho alongside the similarly skilful but physically lightweight Nick Barmby was not working. By the beginning of November Barmby had signed for Everton. Middlesbrough kept losing and slipping down the table.
Since they beat Everton on September 14, Middlesbrough have won just once in 16 league matches and are now propping up the division.

The only bright spots in this long, depressing run, which mirrors a similar nosedive last season, are league cup wins against Newcastle in November and Liverpool earlier this month which have taken them into the semifinals and the threshold of their first major final.
If they did actually win a major trophy for the first time in the same season as going down, it would be a bitter-sweet irony of the cruellest kind.
Whether or not Robson can bring success to a club that seemed poised to do so well or whether he will be the second major managerial casualty in the region this season remains to be seen.

But there are dark clouds gathering down by the Riverside and only a vast improvement on the pitch, starting with a win against Sheffield Wednesday on Saturday, will stop all that Robson has built in the last three years from being blown away.
